title: What an MYP Extended Mathematics Report Card Shows
summary: Learn how an MYP Extended Mathematics report card shows criteria, grades, totals and eAssessment results, with a clear worked grading example.
body_markdown:
An **MYP Extended Mathematics report card** usually shows achievement in four mathematics criteria, an overall grade from **1 to 7** , and teacher feedback. Depending on the school, it may also include a criterion total out of **32** , approaches to learning information, and progress comments.


A school report is not the same as an official **MYP Extended Mathematics eAssessment** result. Internal grades come from evidence assessed by teachers, while the official result comes from an externally marked on-screen examination.


### What appears on an MYP Extended Mathematics report card?


Schools create their own reporting layouts, so there is no single worldwide template. A typical report may include:


- The course name, such as **MYP Extended Mathematics**
- Achievement levels for Criteria A, B, C and D
- A combined criterion total, usually out of **32**
- An overall subject grade from **1 to 7**
- Written feedback describing strengths and next steps
- Approaches to learning, engagement or work-habit indicators
- A provisional eAssessment grade, where applicable


The criterion breakdown is especially useful. The overall grade summarizes attainment, but the four levels reveal whether improvement is needed in mathematical knowledge, investigation, communication or contextual application.


### The four MYP Extended Mathematics criteria


The current[IB MYP Mathematics subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/brochures-and-infographics/pdfs/myp-brief-mathematics-en.pdf) identifies four equally weighted criteria. Each has achievement levels from **0 to 8** , producing a maximum internal total of **32** .


Criterion What it measures


**A: Knowing and understanding** Selecting and applying appropriate mathematics to reach accurate solutions.


**B: Investigating patterns** Identifying relationships, forming rules, testing conjectures and justifying conclusions.


**C: Communicating** Using correct notation, representations and coherent mathematical reasoning.


**D: Applying mathematics in real-life contexts** Modelling authentic situations, solving them and evaluating whether answers are reasonable.


Extended Mathematics contains more demanding content than the standard pathway, but it uses the same four criteria. Accurate calculations are therefore not enough. A correct answer with poorly organized reasoning may provide strong evidence for Criterion A but weaker evidence for Criterion C.


RevisionDojo’s guide to[how MYP Mathematics is assessed](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-myp-mathematics-is-assessed-and-how-to-revise-for-it) explains how students can practise each criterion deliberately.


### How the internal report-card grade is calculated


For criterion-based reporting, the process normally has three stages:


1. The teacher assesses work against the published criterion descriptors.
2. The teacher determines a final **best-fit achievement level** from 0 to 8 for each criterion.
3. The four levels are added and converted into a **1--7 grade** .


Best fit is not necessarily the arithmetic mean of every mark collected. Teachers consider the available evidence and select the descriptor that most accurately represents demonstrated achievement. The school’s assessment policy should explain how recent work, repeated assessments and missing evidence are treated.


The following conversion table is widely used for final MYP criterion totals. Students should still check the school’s policy, especially for interim reports.


Criterion total Final MYP grade


**1--5** **1**


**6--9** **2**


**10--14** **3**


**15--18** **4**


**19--23** **5**


**24--27** **6**


**28--32** **7**


RevisionDojo provides further context in its guide to the[MYP grade boundaries and 1--7 scale](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-myp-grade-boundaries-understanding-the-1-7-scale) . These internal boundaries must not be substituted for official eAssessment boundaries.


### Worked internal grading example


Suppose a report contains these best-fit levels:


Criterion Achievement level


A: Knowing and understanding **7**


B: Investigating patterns **6**


C: Communicating **5**


D: Applying mathematics in real-life contexts **7**


The total is **7 + 6 + 5 + 7 = 25** . Under the table above, **25 out of 32 corresponds to grade 6** .


It should not be interpreted simply as 78.125%, because achievement levels describe performance against rubrics rather than percentage points earned on a conventional test. Criterion C is the lowest result, so useful next steps might include clearer notation, labelled graphs, logical working and explicit explanations.


### What the official eAssessment result shows


The[IB explains that MYP eAssessment](https://ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/assessment-and-exams/) is an optional form of external assessment for most MYP subject groups. Extended Mathematics is assessed through an externally marked on-screen examination.


The examination uses three broad task types:


- Knowing and understanding
- Investigating patterns
- Applying mathematics in real-life contexts


Communication is assessed throughout the examination rather than through one isolated task. All four criteria contribute equally to the assessment design.


The official **MYP Course Results** document records the subject and awarded **1--7 grade** . It should not be expected to reproduce the school report’s four internal criterion levels. The[IB’s MYP regulations](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/become-an-ib-school/pdfs/general-regulations-myp-en.pdf) distinguish classroom assessment from assessments used for official course results.


### How MYP Extended Mathematics grade boundaries work


Official **MYP Extended Mathematics grade boundaries** convert examination performance into a grade from 1 to 7. The IB determines boundaries separately for each examination session through grade-awarding procedures.


Internal school report Official eAssessment result


Uses teacher judgments against criterion descriptors Uses an externally marked on-screen examination


Criterion levels normally total **32** Raw performance uses session-specific boundaries


May include feedback and learning habits Officially reports a **1--7 course grade**


Follows the school’s reporting policy Is awarded by the IB


Boundaries may change because examination papers are not identical in difficulty. Grade awarding aims to keep the standard represented by each grade comparable, so a harder paper may have lower raw-mark boundaries.


For example, imagine that one session placed grade 6 at **72--83** and grade 7 at **84 or above** . A mark of 81 would receive a 6, while 84 would receive a 7. These figures are illustrative only; students must use the official table for the exact subject and examination session.


Students should never apply the internal **28--32 = grade 7** conversion directly to an eAssessment raw mark or assume that a previous session’s boundaries will remain unchanged.


### How to use the report effectively


A report showing **A: 7, B: 4, C: 6 and D: 5** does not mean the student understands a fixed percentage of the course. It shows uneven attainment across four objectives.


A low Criterion B level may indicate difficulty forming or justifying general rules. A low Criterion D level may reveal problems creating models, selecting assumptions or evaluating contextual solutions. Students should:


- Identify the lowest criterion
- Read its descriptor and teacher comments
- Review work that produced the level
- Classify errors as conceptual, procedural, communicative or contextual
- Practise that criterion through unfamiliar questions
- Ask what evidence would meet the next descriptor band


The[RevisionDojo MYP Extended Mathematics resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-extended-mathematics) support targeted topic and criterion practice. Students considering later course choices can also read[whether MYP Extended Mathematics marks matter](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/do-myp-marks-matter-extended-mathematics) .


### Common reporting mistakes


The most common mistake is treating an achievement level out of 8 as a final grade. **Criterion level 6** and **subject grade 6** represent different measurements.


Students should also avoid averaging every task automatically, converting rubric levels into percentages, or using classroom boundaries to predict official results. Extended Mathematics does not award bonus points; its official result remains on the same **1--7 scale** as Mathematics. Reports should label each figure clearly as a raw mark, criterion level, criterion total, predicted grade or official result.


### Conclusion


An MYP Extended Mathematics report card normally shows four criterion levels, a combined total and an overall **1--7 grade** , although schools determine the precise layout. The official eAssessment result is separate and comes from an externally marked on-screen examination using session-specific boundaries.


Students should use the criterion feedback to choose what to practise rather than reducing every result to a percentage. RevisionDojo’s Extended Mathematics Questionbank, Study Notes and[MYP eAssessment study plan](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-eassessments-30-day-study-plan) can support focused preparation.
